title: Severe Hyponatremia as the Initial Sign Preceding Guillain-Barré Syndrome, an Acute Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy: A Case Report
case_prompt:
A 62-year-old woman with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and COPD was found unresponsive at home. One day prior, she reported malaise, decreased appetite, and mild dyspepsia. On arrival, her temperature was normal, blood pressure modestly elevated, and respiratory and heart rates were within normal limits. She was obtunded (GCS 9) and confused. Laboratory studies revealed:  
• WBC 18.1×10^9/L  
• Serum sodium 110 mmol/L (136 mmol/L three months prior)  
• BUN 7 mg/dL, creatinine 0.4 mg/dL  
• Serum glucose 118 mg/dL  
• Serum osmolality 235 mOsm/kg  
• Urine osmolality 413 mOsm/kg, random urine sodium 76 mmol/L  
• Total cholesterol 161 mg/dL, triglycerides 106 mg/dL  
Thyroid-stimulating hormone was 1.0 mIU/L and 8 AM cortisol was 26 mcg/dL. SPEP was negative for monoclonal protein.  
CT of the head and neck, chest radiograph, and ECG were normal. MRI of the brain showed multiple nonspecific T2 hyperintensities without evidence of osmotic demyelination. EEG showed mild diffuse slowing without epileptiform activity.  
A lumbar puncture revealed one nucleated cell and total protein 52 mg/dL; CSF bacterial cultures and viral PCRs were negative.  
In the ICU, losartan and hydrochlorothiazide were held, empiric antibiotics were started, and hypertonic saline was infused. Her serum sodium rose from 110 to 124 mmol/L over 24 hours. By hospital day 5 she was transferred to the ward on fluid restriction and oral sodium chloride.  
On hospital day 6, she developed lower back pain, followed by numbness and tingling in both legs and gait instability. Neurologic examination revealed decreased muscle strength, reduced sensation to light touch, and depressed deep tendon reflexes in both lower extremities.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Considered SIADH due to GBS-related autonomic dysfunction — “damage to those structures from the autoimmune process in GBS can alter ADH release patterns leading to autonomic dysfunction and SIADH.”  
2. Considered thiazide-induced hyponatremia — “given that the patient had been on a stable regimen with unchanged serial sodium levels prior to hospital admission, we feel that this explanation as the primary source of hyponatremia is less likely.”  
3. Excluded hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency — “Thyroid-stimulating hormone and 8 AM cortisol levels were unrevealing (1.0 mIU/L and 26 mcg/dL, resp.).”  
4. Considered pseudohyponatremia from IVIG-induced hyperproteinemia — “While IVIG infusions are prone to causing pseudohyponatremia through delivery of large amounts of proteins, more recent studies have shown that the significant alterations in serum sodium levels cannot completely be explained by this mechanism.”  
5. Excluded central nervous system pathology causing SIADH — “Computed tomography (CT) scan of head and neck, chest X-ray, and electrocardiogram were normal. MRI showed multiple diffuse T2 signal changes in a nonspecific pattern without signs of osmotic demyelination.”
